title: The heartbeat loses its fractal signature with age: HRV detrended fluctuation analysis, validated

dataset.name: Fantasia Database
dataset.record: young (f1y01-05) and elderly (f1o01-05) healthy subjects; RR intervals derived from the ECG
dataset.citation: Iyengar N, Peng CK, Morin R, Goldberger AL, Lipsitz LA. Age-related alterations in the fractal scaling of cardiac interbeat interval dynamics. Am J Physiol 1996;271(4):R1078-R1084. Fantasia Database, PhysioNet (Goldberger et al. 2000).

proposition: A healthy heartbeat is not a metronome and not random noise -- it is FRACTAL, with fluctuations that look statistically similar across time scales. Detrended fluctuation analysis measures this: the short-term scaling exponent alpha1 is a validated cardiac-autonomic and mortality biomarker, sitting near 1.0 (1/f-like fractal dynamics) in a healthy heart and drifting toward 1.5 (smoother, more Brownian, less adaptive) as that fractal organization is lost with aging and disease. On the real Fantasia recordings the signature is unmistakable: alpha1 is 1.05 in the young -- textbook healthy fractal scaling -- and rises to 1.41 in the elderly (an aging effect of +0.36, with every elderly subject above the young mean). And the computation is trustworthy: ecgDFA reproduces an independent, log-spaced standard-DFA implementation (a different least-squares fitter) to MACHINE PRECISION (max |difference| = 1.3x10^-14). The heartbeat loses its fractal signature with age, and the ecosystem measures it correctly.

claims.statement: short-term DFA scaling exponent alpha1 of subject f1y01 (young)
max |ecgDFA - independent standard-DFA| over alpha1/alpha2 (machine precision)
mean DFA alpha1 in the young subjects (healthy fractal scaling ~1.0)
mean DFA alpha1 in the elderly subjects (elevated toward Brownian)
the aging effect on alpha1 (elderly minus young) -- loss of fractal complexity

validation.reference: Detrended fluctuation analysis (Peng et al. 1994/1995) is a standard, exactly-specified algorithm. A correct implementation must reproduce it. The ecosystem's ecgDFA (hand-rolled .fast_lm fitter) matches an INDEPENDENT log-spaced standard-DFA (base stats::lm fitter) to machine precision (max |diff| = 1.3e-14) across all ten Fantasia subjects. The finding -- alpha1 1.05 (young) vs 1.41 (elderly) -- reproduces the established age-related loss of fractal scaling (Iyengar et al. 1996).
validation.data: REAL -- Fantasia (PhysioNet), 5 young + 5 elderly healthy subjects, RR intervals from the ECG
validation.note: The reproducible findings are (1) ecgDFA == an independent standard-DFA to machine precision (max |diff| = 1.3e-14), and (2) the aging effect: alpha1 is higher in the elderly (1.41) than the young (1.05). HONEST scope: (1) the machine-precision claim is against an INDEPENDENT reimplementation (log-spaced scales, base stats::lm -- a different fitter than the package's .fast_lm), which validates the algorithm exactly; against the Python nolds.dfa the agreement is looser (~0.03-0.1, method-dependent windowing) because DFA is implementation-sensitive -- reported, not claimed exact; (2) the aging effect is a demonstration on n=5 + n=5 healthy subjects (all elderly above the young mean, but a small sample) -- the established finding, not a powered clinical study; the young alpha1 range is wide (0.79-1.30); (3) this fold exercises the ecgDFA log-spaced-scales bug fix (PhysioECG 0.3.2): before it, ecgDFA returned NA on these long (2000-9000 beat) RR series because linearly-spaced scales left the alpha1/alpha2 windows underpopulated; (4) run_simulation = FALSE (deterministic).

open_questions.q: alpha1 is a clinical risk marker: below ~0.75 it flags increased mortality after myocardial infarction, and it is the basis of a DFA-a1-guided exercise-intensity method (ecgDFArolling + dfaThresholdCrossings). Extending this validated estimator to a within-subject exercise ramp (does alpha1 fall through the aerobic/anaerobic thresholds?), a post-MI cohort, or a larger age range would turn a validated exponent into a cardiac-risk study. Documented, not escalated.

reference_tools: independent base-R standard DFA (Peng et al. 1994)
